A more recent longitudinal population-based study78 following 148 patients long- term from the onset of epilepsy in childhood found that of 90 patients in whom antiepileptic therapy was stopped, 33 relapsed and although in most cases relapse took place within 3 years, in one case it occurred 28 years after with- drawal. Although these findings indicate that it is often possible to withdraw therapy successfully, it is more difficult to offer an individual prognosis. It has been suggested that adult patients whose livelihood or lifestyle depends on being seizure-free would be generally ill advised to contemplate drug withdrawal.79 Several strategies for predicting the likely outcome after withdrawal of antiepileptic therapy in individuals have been published.80-82 Recognising that ep- ilepsy is a heterogeneous disorder, scoring systems to al- low for various risk factors have been devised.80,81 Prognostic risk factors (some of which are likely to be sur- rogate measures for the underlying condition) may in- clude: • the aetiology of the condition.75,83 Patients classified as having symptomatic or cryptogenic epilepsy generally fare less well than those with idiopathic epilepsy with regard to seizure control, and withdrawal is less likely to be successful • the seizure type and syndrome.75,76,83 A number of stud- ies have identified an increased risk of relapse in pa- tients with particular seizure types; in particular, patients with partial, generalised tonic-clonic, and mixed seizure types seem to be at increased risk. However, it has been pointed out that increased risk has been associated with almost all seizure types other than generalised absence seizures, which seem to have a favourable prognosis; the context in which the seizure arises, such as the asso- ciated epilepsy syndrome and the aetiology, is more im- portant than the type alone when considering withdraw- al.75 Examples of syndromes associated with a favourable outcome for withdrawal include benign childhood epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes, child- hood absence epilepsy, and benign neonatal convul- sions. However, withdrawal is inappropriate in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, despite its good response to treat- ment, as relapse occurs in over 90% of patients • the presence of accompanying neurological or mental deficits.75 Some studies have suggested that mental re- tardation or other neurological deficits are associated with a poorer prognosis on withdrawal; these are proba- bly surrogate markers for symptomatic epilepsy.
